name: Victor Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play hand drums for a community music centre, teach four beginners and sometimes record a simple rhythm for local theatre. I am still a junior player and I learn by watching the senior percussionist set a pace. I like seeing a child hear the whole group; the uneven hours and carrying drums onto the bus are tiring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like around those hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at a school office, and our children are grown and elsewhere. We have a small mortgage and about four months of bills saved, which took effort on ordinary music pay. There are some other music posts nearby, but I do not use AI tools and I would rather talk to a person about a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that a machine filing a booking is fine if it still puts the player’s fee on the sheet. I have no interest in using an AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre classes and my partner’s office hours are steady this term, and four months saved can carry a missed workshop. I still check the mortgage and the bus fares every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the centre’s paid classes, four pupils and theatre calls, and ask for the next term’s playing and preparation fees in writing. In a plateau’s first year I would put one quarter of each cleared extra theatre fee after mortgage, food and bus fares toward six months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this picture. A proper fee sheet makes a routine booking easier to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a computer-made timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if a person checks where I am expected to be and the paid hours. I would not open an AI account to correct the centre’s mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why six months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months helps, but a long gap between terms could take it down quickly. I want a little more room before I promise to stop working.

I would say I have **no interest** in using an AI tool myself.
think: Our **centre classes** and my partner’s hours are steady now.
Four months of **savings** covers some gaps, not a long break.
do: Keep **centre classes and pupils** with theatre calls and written fees this year and through the plateau.
Save **one quarter** of cleared extra theatre fees after essentials toward six months of bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about this term’s work and bills.

fieldNote: He accepts **routine booking software** but has never used AI himself.

Save quarter of cleared extra theatre fees after mortgage, food and buses toward six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the musicians’ association to show us what happens to paid booking and preparation hours. One junior player arguing alone will not set the centre’s rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre may book fewer teaching hours, and local theatre may buy generated rhythms. That would cut my own pay, even if the drum itself still needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the musicians’ association to meet the centre about a written minimum for class preparation and cancellations, and keep the paid classes and four pupils. If two monthly theatre calls disappear, I would seek an advertised paid community-centre programme assistant job only if secondary schooling is accepted and written net pay after bus fares replaces the loss; I would keep music work until a signed offer, and repeat that check in the first year of disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours going down. Four months saved buys a little search time, not a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee sheets for the last two terms and the hours we prepared without pay. A meeting needs numbers, not a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid office training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not while losing a paid class to do it. I would ask whether a real vacancy accepts my secondary schooling before changing my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that thinking AGI could book and make rhythm tracks in 2028, while robot drummers come around 2031. I want the paid hours put plainly on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the theatre calls to stop and perhaps one of my centre classes to be cut. That is a piece of the mortgage payment, even with four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would have the association ask for written class and cancellation rates and keep four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if theatre calls end and a centre class is cut, I would seek an actual posted paid programme assistant vacancy accepting my secondary education only if its written net wage after bus fares replaces the lost music pay; I would keep remaining classes and pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing those hours quickly. I still have a few months to apply, and some local posts exist if an employer actually advertises one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your association block the job move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I can defend music fees with the association while I look after my household. Those two things can happen together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the later robot date change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still expect human drumming on stage until around 2031 in this picture. The booking and cheap tracks could take money in 2028, so the contract matters first.

I would ask the **centre** to put paid hours plainly on paper.

Our **four-month cushion** buys search time, not security forever.

Seek **posted programme vacancy** after 2028 theatre/class losses, with accepted schooling and written replacement net after buses.

fieldNote: He expects **2028 desk-work losses** before robot drumming around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the association that five years is time to put a fair preparation rate into centre contracts. Thinking AGI is around 2031, and robot drummers around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theatre recordings may still go, but I could earn more steady hours at the community centre if a real paid programme post opens. I do not want to learn a tool that would only hide unpaid planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep classes and pupils, and bring last term’s unpaid preparation hours to the association’s centre meeting. If two theatre calls disappear, I would watch for a posted paid programme assistant vacancy, check that my secondary schooling qualifies and get the written net wage after buses before accepting; in the first year after 2031 I would move only if that wage replaces lost music pay and keep current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely recording losses, though five years gives us room to negotiate and look for a post. I would rather work a paid centre desk than sit through unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need another certificate for that desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the actual vacancy first. If it needs a certificate, I would ask for funded training on paid time before making a promise or giving up music hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no centre post opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid classes and pupils and ask the association to keep pressing for fair fees. A plan cannot manufacture a paid programme-assistant vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot drummers around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask the centre to write down every paid hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might choose fewer late shows, but I have no retirement date set. Four months saved and the mortgage mean our current pay matters through the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid centre classes, four pupils and theatre calls, and save a quarter of cleared extra theatre fees after mortgage, food and buses toward six months of bills. Across the decade I would ask the association for written minimum preparation and cancellation pay; in the first year after 2036, if theatre and centre hours fall, I would seek a posted paid programme assistant role only if my secondary education is accepted or any required certificate is funded on paid time, and a written net wage after buses replaces the loss, keeping music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of paid recordings. For the next few years our current classes, partner’s wage and four months saved hold the mortgage, though I still check every term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why no retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not worked out whether the pay and savings will support one. I will look at the actual bills and health then, not announce a birthday as a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the association wins no new rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the existing paid hours and look at real posted jobs if work shrinks. I would not count a future association fee agreement as money in the account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recording calls and a class could vanish before I can replace their pay. Written centre fees, association help and a real posted assistant job at a net wage that covers the loss would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who counts preparation when a class is cancelled. A drum class does not begin when the children walk in; I have carried and set up the kit already.

headlineQuote: A drum class does not begin when the children walk in; I have carried and set up the kit already.
portrait: Victor is a **junior percussionist** still learning, with secondary schooling and typical music pay.
He has **four months saved**, a school-office partner, grown children and a small mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and looks to the musicians’ association for written preparation pay.
He considers **paid programme work** only after music losses and a qualifying written replacement offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove theatre calls and a centre class before wages replace them.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written centre fees**, association help and an actual paid vacancy with replacement net wages.
